nameStory: Greater duckweed gets its name from being a favorite food of ducks and other waterfowl, who gobble it up like green floating snacks. The 'greater' part comes from it being the largest of the common duckweeds you'll find floating on New England ponds. It's also called 'duckmeat' for the same reason – it's like a floating salad bar for our feathered friends!
description: Greater duckweed is a tiny floating plant that looks like little green coins scattered across the water's surface. Each plant is actually just a single flat, oval leaf (called a frond) about the size of your pinky nail, with several white roots dangling underneath like tiny streamers. These plants often form dense green carpets that can cover entire ponds or quiet stream backwaters. Despite being so small, they're actually flowering plants, though their flowers are so tiny you'd need a magnifying glass to see them.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Flat, oval-shaped green 'leaves' about 3-8mm across that feel smooth and slightly thick, like tiny succulent leaves. Each frond has 3-5 distinct veins visible when held up to light.

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Multiple white thread-like roots (usually 5-15) dangle from each frond's underside, feeling soft and feathery when touched gently.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Floats freely on water surface, often forming dense mats. Individual plants connect by thin stalks but break apart easily when disturbed.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to medium green on top, often with a reddish or purplish tinge on the underside, especially in cooler weather.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Larger than other duckweeds – about the size of a small button or your pinky nail, making it easy to spot among smaller floating plants.

habitat: Look for greater duckweed floating on quiet freshwater surfaces throughout New England – ponds, slow streams, marshes, and protected coves of lakes. It thrives in nutrient-rich water and prefers spots with little current where it won't get swept away. You'll often find it mixed with other aquatic plants in shallow areas that warm up nicely in the sun.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge from winter dormancy and begin rapid growth as water temperatures warm. Look for small green patches starting to spread across quiet water surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when dense green mats cover large areas of suitable habitat. Plants reproduce rapidly by budding, creating the thick carpets you'll see on many ponds.
seasonality.fall: Plants may develop reddish undersides as temperatures cool. Growth slows and plants begin forming winter buds (turions) that will sink and overwinter.
seasonality.winter: Most plants die back, but hardy winter buds rest on the bottom until spring. Some plants may persist under ice in protected spots with moving water.

funFact: Greater duckweed is one of the world's smallest flowering plants, yet it's also one of the fastest-growing – a single plant can multiply into millions within months, making it capable of doubling its population every 2-3 days under ideal conditions!
confusionNotes: Often confused with lesser duckweed, but greater duckweed is noticeably larger and has multiple roots per plant (lesser duckweed has just one). Remember: 'Greater' = bigger fronds and MORE roots dangling below like a tiny octopus.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its simple appearance, greater duckweed is actually a sophisticated plant in the arum family, making it a distant relative of jack-in-the-pulpit and skunk cabbage. Many people think duckweeds are algae or moss, but they're true flowering plants with roots, stems, and leaves – they're just highly specialized for aquatic life.
compareHints: Since greater duckweed is the only Spirodela species common in New England, compare it with other duckweeds in the broader duckweed family. It's the giant of the group – larger fronds and multiple roots make it easy to distinguish from the smaller, single-rooted lesser duckweed. Think of it as the 'big sibling' among the floating duckweed family.
